after.text:
In order to obtain a useful bound from Lemma 8.3, we need to give a non-trivial
bound for the product over j appearing there (which will be an easy calculation using
Lemma 8.2), and we need a good bound for Jk,r (N 2/5 ). We also cannot succeed unless
k is chosen suitably large, since the applications of Hölder’s inequality in the proof
of Lemma 8.3 are very inefficient unless Jk,r (λ1 , ..., λr ; N 2/5 ) ≈ Jk,r (N 2/5 ) for most
λ1 , ..., λr , which can only happen if k is large in terms of r. In the next section we will
study Jk,r (N 2/5 ), and this will occupy most of the rest of Chapter 2.

section_entries.label: 10. Second thoughts on estimating zeta sums

neighboring_unit_entries.title: A rational-approximation degree window converts mean-value savings into zeta-sum cancellation
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: After setting k proportional to r², the mean-value theorem supplies a global negative exponent. For degrees in a selected window, the explicit Taylor coefficients admit rational approximants with denominators in a favorable range, giving extra spacing savings; choosing the proportionality constant controls delta and makes the negative term dominate losses.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: Block decomposition transfers short-sum cancellation to a near-one-line zeta bound
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: The Hardy–Littlewood approximation is split into exponentially sized blocks; Abel summation imports the zeta-sum estimate into each weighted block, and a second grouping makes the block series summable. A different splitting point handles sigma farther from one.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The right diagnostic for the theorem is its cancellation range: fixed-power blocks receive a power saving, while subpower blocks retain only a weaker nontrivial gain down to the method's exponential threshold.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Setting M=N=t^θ in Theorem 10.1 turns its exponential factor into N^{-cθ²}, hence a bound N^{1-cθ²}; when N is smaller than every fixed power of t but exceeds exp(C(log t)^{2/3}), the theorem is still nontrivial but no longer gives a power saving.
directed.conceptual_reading: Scale interpretation distinguishes the strength of cancellation from the mere existence of a bound and locates where the degree growth of the earlier polynomialization begins to dominate.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The substitution N=t^θ translates an exponential expression in log N and log t into an ordinary power exponent, making the theorem comparable with the square-root-cancellation benchmark.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The result remains far above the heuristic N^{1/2+o(1)} square-root scale, and below the stated threshold the N^{4/5} term prevents this argument from providing the claimed nontrivial control.
directed.uncertainty: The qualitative scale distinction is explicit; constants in the lower threshold are not resolved in this short interpretive span.

supported: For M=N=t^θ the source obtains N^{1-cθ²}, hence a power saving at every fixed positive θ.
It contrasts this with the N^{1/2+o(1)} random-oscillation benchmark and says that a subpower but above-threshold range still receives a nontrivial, non-power saving.
inference: Substituting N=t^θ is correctly identified as the representation change that turns the logarithmic exponential into an ordinary power.
unsupported_or_imported: The statement that this scale transition locates where degree growth from polynomialization begins to dominate is imported from earlier mechanism rather than stated in this span.

The claim that the N^{4/5} remainder prevents nontrivial control below the threshold gives the wrong obstruction: that term is itself smaller than N; the span merely makes no nontrivial-range claim below the threshold, while the exponential saving becomes too weak.
